analysis.one_liner: Lets college athletes cash in on endorsement deals while barring them from ever becoming paid employees of their schools.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan pair introduced the bill on June 9, 2025 and it has sat in two House committees with no action and no cosponsors beyond one Democrat since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write national rules for college athletes' name, image, and likeness (NIL) deals. It says schools, conferences, and the NCAA cannot block an athlete from signing an endorsement contract, guarantees athletes the right to hire agents, and orders college sports governing bodies to build a public database of what NIL deals actually pay. It also ties federal Education Department funding to new school obligations: colleges would have to cover an athlete's sports-related medical bills for four years after they leave, guarantee four-year scholarships, and let injured athletes keep their scholarship money. But the same bill declares that student athletes are not employees of their schools or the NCAA, wipes out state laws that regulate athlete pay more strictly, and gives schools and the NCAA legal immunity for following the rules in the bill.
analysis.who_benefits: College athletes on varsity teams. They would gain a federally protected right to sign endorsement deals, a right to professional representation, a public database showing market rates for NIL contracts, four years of post-graduation medical coverage for sports injuries, and scholarships that cannot be reduced or canceled because of injury, illness, performance, or roster cuts.

how_it_helps.text: No school, conference, or national athletic association could restrict an athlete's ability to enter an NIL agreement, except for deals that violate the school's conduct code, damage the school's reputation, or conflict with an existing school contract.

Colleges would have to pay all medical costs from sports injuries for four years after an athlete graduates or leaves, and could not reduce or cancel an athletic scholarship for athletic performance, injury, illness, or roster-management decisions.
An athletic scholarship would remain available for degree completion for ten years after it was first agreed to, even if the athlete stops playing.
National athletic associations would have to maintain a public, searchable database of anonymized NIL deal terms so athletes and their agents can estimate fair market value before signing.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges and universities bear new costs: four years of post-graduation medical coverage for sports injuries, guaranteed multi-year scholarships, and mandatory education programs. In exchange, athletes give up any claim to employee status, stronger state NIL laws are wiped out, and schools that comply with the bill get a broad shield against lawsuits under other laws.

drawbacks.text: Section 9 declares that a student athlete can never be considered an employee of their school, conference, or national athletic association based on playing a sport. That closes off the main legal route athletes have used to argue for direct pay, benefits, or union representation.

Section 9 preempts state laws governing athlete compensation, employment status, or eligibility, which would override stricter state-level protections, such as laws some states passed to expand athlete pay rights.

Section 8 says an institution, conference, or association that complies with the bill cannot be treated as violating any other law or regulation or face liability under them, limiting athletes' ability to challenge college sports rules in court.
Schools could still disqualify an athlete's NIL deal if it 'negatively impacts the reputation or public image' of the institution, a vague standard that lets schools police deals they dislike.

Conferences could still bar or limit compensation to athletes intended to induce a transfer between schools, and any NIL agreement that fails the bill's writing and disclosure requirements is void from the start.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The athlete protections are real and specific: guaranteed endorsements, agent access, market transparency, injury medical coverage, and scholarship security. But the bill buys those protections by giving college sports governing bodies their two biggest legal asks — permanent non-employee status for athletes and federal preemption of state law — plus a liability shield. An athlete who wanted direct pay or a union would walk away with less legal standing than before. Whether the trade is fair depends on how much you value the named protections against the rights it forecloses.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2025 and referred to two House committees, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Lisa McClain introduced the bill for herself and Rep. Janelle Bynum on June 9, 2025.
Bynum, a Democrat, is the bill's single cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee.
No further action has been taken since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody yet. The current arrangement — where the NCAA and conferences write their own NIL rules and athletes have no federal protections — continues unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the status quo holds

for.name: Rep. Lisa McClain
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House on June 9, 2025.

for.name: Rep. Janelle Bynum
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the bill's only cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: Only two members are attached — a Republican sponsor and a single Democratic cosponsor — so no partisan pattern has emerged yet, and no one has opposed it on the record.

industries.industry: College sports governing bodies (the NCAA and major conferences)
industries.note: The bill hands these associations their core legislative goals: athletes are declared never-employees, state laws regulating athlete pay are preempted, and compliant associations get a shield from liability under other laws. In return they must register NIL agents and publish a market-value database. This locks in the amateurism model — athlete earnings flow through third-party endorsements, never from the schools — even as it guarantees athletes some rights within it.

Schools would take on real new obligations: four years of post-separation medical coverage for sports injuries, scholarships that cannot be cut for injury or performance, ten-year degree-completion funding, and mandatory athlete education. In exchange they gain the same liability shield and federal preemption, plus a funding lever run by the Education Department.

industries.industry: NIL marketing agencies and athlete agents
industries.note: The bill creates a formal registration system run by the athletic associations and a public market-value database, giving agents and marketers a clearer, more established marketplace to operate in.

analysis.trajectory: With only one cosponsor, no committee action months after introduction, and a split referral across two committees, the bill is unlikely to advance unless House leadership or the relevant chairs prioritize it. Most bills at this stage die quietly in committee.
